sources.title: Experts weigh in: “How can I get my young child less anxious about starting school?”
sources.publisher: Understood (experts including Janine Domingues, Child Mind Institute, and Brian Stack)
sources.quote: If possible, plan a visit to the school with your child. It can be helpful to take pictures of the school and classroom, as well as the adults your child will work with. You can show the pictures in the days and weeks leading up to school to help familiarize your child with this new environment. ... Let your child know that it’s normal to feel anxious about starting school. Acknowledging fears can be helpful. For example, you can try saying, “You may be feeling nervous or scared about starting school, and that’s OK. You can get through it, and I’m here to help.” Reaching out to friends who may be in the same class and setting up playdates prior to school starting can also help ease worries. And providing your child with positive praise for coping with nervousness will help with building good coping skills. ... It’s also common to see physical symptoms of anxiety. Your child may have a stomachache, usually in the morning before school or in the evening before going to bed. ... Most young children are creatures of habit and thrive on routines and schedules. Starting school changes what they’ve come to expect with their predictable lifestyle. ... They may feel insecure about the school and classroom environments. There may be some who are anxious about something as simple as eating lunch at school or using a bathroom that they’re not familiar with. ... Kids can feed off of parents’ anxiety. Do your best to be calm and routine when preparing for back to school. Don’t make a big deal out of it.
sources.supports: Visiting the school and photographing it, saying that nervousness is normal and that you are there to help, a playdate with a classmate before school, praise for coping, a stomachache as a common sign, children who thrive on routine, worries about unfamiliar bathrooms and being calm about it. An article of expert answers on a parent site, applied to Israeli first graders as general advice.

sources.title: Preparing for 1st Grade
sources.publisher: Scholastic Parents (Michele Myers, Ph.D., Wake Forest University)
sources.quote: Build independence. It can be tempting to swoop in and do most things for younger kids. Resist the urge! Encouraging kids to practice independence and learn from their mistakes builds essential skills and boosts their confidence. “You can aid your child in this regard by letting them practice daily routines like getting dressed, packing a bag, making a snack, or tidying up their own rooms,” says Myers. “Encourage them to do things for themselves and celebrate their efforts and growing independence.” ... Prioritize sleep. “Sleep is essential to a child’s overall well-being,” says Myers. “It directly affects their physical, emotional, and mental growth.” She suggests setting a regular bedtime and morning routine before school starts in order to make the transition easier.
sources.supports: Letting a child practise getting dressed and packing a bag by themselves and celebrating the effort; a regular bedtime and morning routine before school starts. An article by an education professor for American parents, applied as general advice.

sources.title: 5 Ways Books Can Help Your Anxious Child
sources.publisher: PBS KIDS for Parents
sources.quote: Use books to ignite a conversation to help children process feelings. Young children are still learning how to process big emotions. They might not have all the tools or words yet to explain how and why they are feeling a certain way. Allow books to bridge that gap. If you suspect your child might be struggling, pick up a children’s book at your local library in which the main character is experiencing the same emotion. You might find your little one is able to talk about the story, and, in doing so, make connections to their own emotions.
sources.supports: A story with a main character who feels the same thing can help a young child talk about their own feelings. The page is about anxious children; used only as support for reading a story about a hard moment, with no promise of a result.

sources.title: Experts weigh in: “How can I get my young child less anxious about starting school?”
sources.publisher: Understood (experts including Janine Domingues, Child Mind Institute, and Brian Stack)
sources.quote: If possible, plan a visit to the school with your child. It can be helpful to take pictures of the school and classroom, as well as the adults your child will work with. You can show the pictures in the days and weeks leading up to school to help familiarize your child with this new environment. ... Let your child know that it’s normal to feel anxious about starting school. Acknowledging fears can be helpful. For example, you can try saying, “You may be feeling nervous or scared about starting school, and that’s OK. You can get through it, and I’m here to help.” Reaching out to friends who may be in the same class and setting up playdates prior to school starting can also help ease worries. And providing your child with positive praise for coping with nervousness will help with building good coping skills. ... It’s also common to see physical symptoms of anxiety. Your child may have a stomachache, usually in the morning before school or in the evening before going to bed. ... Most young children are creatures of habit and thrive on routines and schedules. Starting school changes what they’ve come to expect with their predictable lifestyle. ... They may feel insecure about the school and classroom environments. There may be some who are anxious about something as simple as eating lunch at school or using a bathroom that they’re not familiar with. ... Kids can feed off of parents’ anxiety. Do your best to be calm and routine when preparing for back to school. Don’t make a big deal out of it.
sources.supports: Visiting the school and photographing it, saying that nervousness is normal and that you are there to help, a playdate with a classmate before school, praise for coping, a stomachache as a common sign, children who thrive on routine, worries about unfamiliar bathrooms and being calm about it. An article of expert answers on a parent site, applied to Israeli first graders as general advice.

sources.title: Preparing for 1st Grade
sources.publisher: Scholastic Parents (Michele Myers, Ph.D., Wake Forest University)
sources.quote: Build independence. It can be tempting to swoop in and do most things for younger kids. Resist the urge! Encouraging kids to practice independence and learn from their mistakes builds essential skills and boosts their confidence. “You can aid your child in this regard by letting them practice daily routines like getting dressed, packing a bag, making a snack, or tidying up their own rooms,” says Myers. “Encourage them to do things for themselves and celebrate their efforts and growing independence.” ... Prioritize sleep. “Sleep is essential to a child’s overall well-being,” says Myers. “It directly affects their physical, emotional, and mental growth.” She suggests setting a regular bedtime and morning routine before school starts in order to make the transition easier.
sources.supports: Letting a child practise getting dressed and packing a bag by themselves and celebrating the effort; a regular bedtime and morning routine before school starts. An article by an education professor for American parents, applied as general advice.

sources.title: 5 Ways Books Can Help Your Anxious Child
sources.publisher: PBS KIDS for Parents
sources.quote: Use books to ignite a conversation to help children process feelings. Young children are still learning how to process big emotions. They might not have all the tools or words yet to explain how and why they are feeling a certain way. Allow books to bridge that gap. If you suspect your child might be struggling, pick up a children’s book at your local library in which the main character is experiencing the same emotion. You might find your little one is able to talk about the story, and, in doing so, make connections to their own emotions.
sources.supports: A story with a main character who feels the same thing can help a young child talk about their own feelings. The page is about anxious children; used only as support for reading a story about a hard moment, with no promise of a result.

sources.title: Experts weigh in: “How can I get my young child less anxious about starting school?”
sources.publisher: Understood (experts including Janine Domingues, Child Mind Institute, and Brian Stack)
sources.quote: If possible, plan a visit to the school with your child. It can be helpful to take pictures of the school and classroom, as well as the adults your child will work with. You can show the pictures in the days and weeks leading up to school to help familiarize your child with this new environment. ... Let your child know that it’s normal to feel anxious about starting school. Acknowledging fears can be helpful. For example, you can try saying, “You may be feeling nervous or scared about starting school, and that’s OK. You can get through it, and I’m here to help.” Reaching out to friends who may be in the same class and setting up playdates prior to school starting can also help ease worries. And providing your child with positive praise for coping with nervousness will help with building good coping skills. ... It’s also common to see physical symptoms of anxiety. Your child may have a stomachache, usually in the morning before school or in the evening before going to bed. ... Most young children are creatures of habit and thrive on routines and schedules. Starting school changes what they’ve come to expect with their predictable lifestyle. ... They may feel insecure about the school and classroom environments. There may be some who are anxious about something as simple as eating lunch at school or using a bathroom that they’re not familiar with. ... Kids can feed off of parents’ anxiety. Do your best to be calm and routine when preparing for back to school. Don’t make a big deal out of it.
sources.supports: Visiting the school and photographing it, saying that nervousness is normal and that you are there to help, a playdate with a classmate before school, praise for coping, a stomachache as a common sign, children who thrive on routine, worries about unfamiliar bathrooms and being calm about it. An article of expert answers on a parent site, applied to Israeli first graders as general advice.

sources.title: Preparing for 1st Grade
sources.publisher: Scholastic Parents (Michele Myers, Ph.D., Wake Forest University)
sources.quote: Build independence. It can be tempting to swoop in and do most things for younger kids. Resist the urge! Encouraging kids to practice independence and learn from their mistakes builds essential skills and boosts their confidence. “You can aid your child in this regard by letting them practice daily routines like getting dressed, packing a bag, making a snack, or tidying up their own rooms,” says Myers. “Encourage them to do things for themselves and celebrate their efforts and growing independence.” ... Prioritize sleep. “Sleep is essential to a child’s overall well-being,” says Myers. “It directly affects their physical, emotional, and mental growth.” She suggests setting a regular bedtime and morning routine before school starts in order to make the transition easier.
sources.supports: Letting a child practise getting dressed and packing a bag by themselves and celebrating the effort; a regular bedtime and morning routine before school starts. An article by an education professor for American parents, applied as general advice.

sources.title: 5 Ways Books Can Help Your Anxious Child
sources.publisher: PBS KIDS for Parents
sources.quote: Use books to ignite a conversation to help children process feelings. Young children are still learning how to process big emotions. They might not have all the tools or words yet to explain how and why they are feeling a certain way. Allow books to bridge that gap. If you suspect your child might be struggling, pick up a children’s book at your local library in which the main character is experiencing the same emotion. You might find your little one is able to talk about the story, and, in doing so, make connections to their own emotions.
sources.supports: A story with a main character who feels the same thing can help a young child talk about their own feelings. The page is about anxious children; used only as support for reading a story about a hard moment, with no promise of a result.

sources.title: Emotional Issues and Potty Training Problems
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 25 May 2022; adapted from the AAP Guide to Toilet Training, 2nd Edition)
sources.quote: At about three years of age, children start developing the capacity to experience discomfort, or shame, when they have done something they know is wrong. ... They may hide their wet underwear, or even try to clean up the mess before you see it. There is no cause to criticize or punish a child who behaves in this way. ... The best response when you find your child hiding their accidents from you is to gently tell them that you know they had an accident, that it’s okay, and that you know they will do better next time. Then ask them to help you clean up, and talk with them about specific ways the two of you can help them get back on track. ... If they feel you have been too controlling about bathroom use—constantly asking if they need to go instead of letting them direct their own behavior—they may resist going until it’s too late and they have an accident instead. ... Respond calmly and use it as an opportunity to support and communicate with your child. ... Meanwhile, try to avoid major concessions such as returning to diapers. Instead, consider offering to put them in training pants under their underwear for a while, put the potty in their room, accompany them to the preschool bathroom before the school day begins, or otherwise compromise until they feel more secure.
sources.supports: Around age three a child can feel shame after an accident and may hide it; do not criticise or punish, say gently that it is okay, ask the child to help clean up; constant asking can backfire; respond calmly; avoid going back to diapers, offer training pants under underwear and the potty in the child's room. A pediatrics academy page, applied as general child health advice.

sources.title: Potty Training Regression
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 25 May 2022; adapted from the AAP Guide to Toilet Training, 2nd Edition)
sources.quote: For young children, though, learning often depends on their development in other areas. They often progress in a series of sudden spurts interspersed with periods of little apparent improvement. At times, a child may even regress in their learning—that is, lose skills they recently acquired or even take a few steps back in their learning process. ... Common causes of potty training regression in young children include: Change in the child-care routine—for example, a new sitter, or starting a child-care or preschool program ... If there is no physical reason, let your child know that you’ve noticed their change in behavior ... Ask them why this might be ... Listen to their response, and help them try to communicate any events that are upsetting them, as well as their feelings about them. ... Support them with positive reinforcements, including hugs and praise, stickers on a chart, and an occasional pep talk as they struggle to regain their footing. ... Upsetting as regression can be to parents, it usually doesn’t last very long. In many cases, the child picks up where she left off in toilet training after a few days or weeks.
sources.supports: Learning to use the toilet comes in spurts and can slip back; a change in routine is a common cause; ask the child and listen; praise and a pep talk; it usually passes in a few days or weeks. A pediatrics academy page, applied to Israeli families as general child health advice.

sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by KidsHealth Medical Experts, March 2019)

Reassure your child that he or she is well on the way to using the potty like a big kid. ... Many kids who've been using the potty have some trouble during times of stress.

sources.title: 5 Ways Books Can Help Your Anxious Child

sources.title: Emotional Issues and Potty Training Problems
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 25 May 2022; adapted from the AAP Guide to Toilet Training, 2nd Edition)
sources.quote: At about three years of age, children start developing the capacity to experience discomfort, or shame, when they have done something they know is wrong. ... They may hide their wet underwear, or even try to clean up the mess before you see it. There is no cause to criticize or punish a child who behaves in this way. ... The best response when you find your child hiding their accidents from you is to gently tell them that you know they had an accident, that it’s okay, and that you know they will do better next time. Then ask them to help you clean up, and talk with them about specific ways the two of you can help them get back on track. ... If they feel you have been too controlling about bathroom use—constantly asking if they need to go instead of letting them direct their own behavior—they may resist going until it’s too late and they have an accident instead. ... Respond calmly and use it as an opportunity to support and communicate with your child. ... Meanwhile, try to avoid major concessions such as returning to diapers. Instead, consider offering to put them in training pants under their underwear for a while, put the potty in their room, accompany them to the preschool bathroom before the school day begins, or otherwise compromise until they feel more secure.
sources.supports: Around age three a child can feel shame after an accident and may hide it; do not criticise or punish, say gently that it is okay, ask the child to help clean up; constant asking can backfire; respond calmly; avoid going back to diapers, offer training pants under underwear and the potty in the child's room. A pediatrics academy page, applied as general child health advice.

sources.title: Potty Training Regression
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 25 May 2022; adapted from the AAP Guide to Toilet Training, 2nd Edition)
sources.quote: For young children, though, learning often depends on their development in other areas. They often progress in a series of sudden spurts interspersed with periods of little apparent improvement. At times, a child may even regress in their learning—that is, lose skills they recently acquired or even take a few steps back in their learning process. ... Common causes of potty training regression in young children include: Change in the child-care routine—for example, a new sitter, or starting a child-care or preschool program ... If there is no physical reason, let your child know that you’ve noticed their change in behavior ... Ask them why this might be ... Listen to their response, and help them try to communicate any events that are upsetting them, as well as their feelings about them. ... Support them with positive reinforcements, including hugs and praise, stickers on a chart, and an occasional pep talk as they struggle to regain their footing. ... Upsetting as regression can be to parents, it usually doesn’t last very long. In many cases, the child picks up where she left off in toilet training after a few days or weeks.
sources.supports: Learning to use the toilet comes in spurts and can slip back; a change in routine is a common cause; ask the child and listen; praise and a pep talk; it usually passes in a few days or weeks. A pediatrics academy page, applied to Israeli families as general child health advice.

sources.title: Potty Training
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by KidsHealth Medical Experts, March 2019)
sources.quote: Praise all attempts to use the toilet, even if nothing happens. And remember that accidents will happen. It's important not to punish potty-training children or show disappointment when they wet or soil themselves or the bed. Instead, tell your child that it was an accident and offer your support. Reassure your child that he or she is well on the way to using the potty like a big kid. ... Many kids who've been using the potty have some trouble during times of stress.
sources.supports: Praise every attempt, accidents happen, do not punish or show disappointment, say it was an accident and offer support; trouble during stress is common. A children's hospital health page, applied as general advice.

sources.title: 5 Ways Books Can Help Your Anxious Child
sources.publisher: PBS KIDS for Parents
sources.quote: Use books to ignite a conversation to help children process feelings. Young children are still learning how to process big emotions. They might not have all the tools or words yet to explain how and why they are feeling a certain way. Allow books to bridge that gap. If you suspect your child might be struggling, pick up a children’s book at your local library in which the main character is experiencing the same emotion. You might find your little one is able to talk about the story, and, in doing so, make connections to their own emotions.
sources.supports: A story with a main character who feels the same thing can help a young child talk about their own feelings. The page is about anxious children; used only as support for reading a story about a hard moment, with no promise of a result.
